name: ArchiveBox
purpose: Self-hosted web-archiving application that takes URLs from many input formats and saves each as HTML, PDF, screenshot, WARC, SingleFile, readability text, media and more, with a browsable index.
journalism_use_case: Build your own tamper-evident archive of official pages and documents on a schedule, so that when an agency rewrites or deletes a page you hold dated local copies rather than depending on a third-party archive — and because it saves several formats per URL, you have both a readable copy and a WARC.
pros: Multi-format capture per URL is the distinguishing feature: a PDF for an editor, a screenshot for a story, a WARC for evidence, and readability text for search — all from one ingest
Everything stored on your own disk by default, with a browsable index that a non-engineer can use
Very large community (29,045 stars) and active development (pushed 2026-11-17, release v0.9.77 2026-10-27)
Accepts input from browser bookmarks, RSS, text files and more, so getting URLs in is never the obstacle
cons: Not a change-detection tool: it captures and preserves, and diffing between snapshots is explicitly not its job — pair it with webchanges or EDGI tooling for monitoring
Heavy dependency surface (Chromium/Playwright, wget, curl, yt-dlp, singlefile, readability and other extractor binaries), so installs break and upgrades need care
Long-running release-candidate versions (current tag v0.9.78rc242) blur the stable/unstable line and make pinning a judgement call
Archive size grows quickly with multi-format capture — storage planning is a real requirement, not an afterthought
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 29,045 stars with 157 open issues, release v0.9.77 (2026-10-27), current tag v0.9.78rc242, pushed 2026-11-17. The extended release-candidate numbering is visible in the tag itself and is a genuine versioning concern for operators.
assessment: My recommended default for a newsroom's own archive of source pages, because the multi-format output serves the editorial, evidentiary and search needs simultaneously. For your profile: pin to a stable release rather than an rc tag, plan storage explicitly (multi-format capture is several times the page size), and keep the instance internal — an exposed ArchiveBox index is a list of everything your newsroom has found interesting. Note the optional extractors that can submit URLs to the Internet Archive; disable those for sensitive targets.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.9.77 (2026-10-27), current tag v0.9.78rc242, 29,045 stars, 157 open issues. Same-day commits and recent releases with a very large community; the prolonged rc series is a release-engineering characteristic rather than a decline signal.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Archived content belongs to the original publishers.
licence_restrictions: None material. Note the bundled extractors carry their own licences (yt-dlp is Unlicense, SingleFile AGPL-3.0), which matters only if you redistribute a bundle.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a container host plus substantial storage — budget several times the raw page size per URL because of multi-format capture; a few thousand pages with media can reach hundreds of GB. Assumptions: self-hosted Docker, default extractor set.
privacy: Everything is stored on your own disk by default. Two things to control: optional extractors can submit URLs to the Internet Archive (disclosing your interest to a third party and making the URL public), and the index itself is a sensitive artefact that must not be publicly reachable.
alternatives: Browsertrix (platform) for team-scale crawling with managed replay
Scoop for single-page captures with provenance attestation
pywb plus browsertrix-crawler for a WARC-first architecture
summary: Self-hosted web-archiving application that takes URLs from many input formats and saves each as HTML, PDF, screenshot, WARC…

name: browsertrix-crawler
purpose: Dockerised browser-based crawler that drives Chromium to produce high-fidelity WARC/WACZ captures, with configurable scope, behaviours for dynamic pages and sitemap support.
journalism_use_case: Capture modern government portals, dashboards and interactive document viewers faithfully enough that the archived copy still behaves like the live page when a disputed change is later examined — the capture tool of record for anything built as a single-page application.
pros: Highest practical capture fidelity in this catalogue for dynamic content, because it records what a real browser actually fetched and rendered
Single Docker image with declarative configuration, which makes it dramatically easier to operate than brozzler for comparable capability
WACZ output is a single portable file that ReplayWeb.page can open with no server, so sharing a capture with an editor or lawyer is trivial
Very actively maintained (v1.15.4, 2026-11-11) by the organisation that defines much of current web-archiving practice
cons: No change detection or alerting — it is capture infrastructure, so monitoring must be built around it
Resource-hungry: browser-based capture is far slower and more memory-intensive per page than static crawling, which caps throughput
AGPL-3.0 has network-service implications if you expose a modified version, which is worth a legal check before building a capture service for partners
Requires Docker familiarity and 152 open issues reflect the complexity of behaviours across many site types
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,197 stars with 152 open issues, release v1.15.4 (2026-11-11), pushed 2026-11-14. Webrecorder's tooling is the de facto standard in modern web archiving, verifiable from IIPC and institutional archive adoption.
assessment: Adopt as your capture tool of record for anything dynamic or disputed. For your profile the combination that works is browsertrix-crawler for capture, WACZ as the artefact, and ReplayWeb.page for handing a capture to a colleague or lawyer who has no infrastructure. Write the capture configuration into version control alongside the investigation notes, so the methodology is reproducible — that is what makes the capture defensible rather than merely good.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v1.15.4 (2026-11-11), 1,197 stars, 152 open issues. Frequent releases from a funded organisation whose core mission this is.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Captured content belongs to the original publishers.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: offering a modified version as a network service obliges source publication. Running it internally to produce captures carries no obligation.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a Docker host with several GB of RAM per concurrent browser plus storage for WACZ output; capture throughput is low enough that large crawls need either patience or parallel workers. Assumptions: self-hosted, moderate crawl sizes.
privacy: WARC/WACZ output is written to storage you control (local disk or S3-compatible); nothing is sent to Webrecorder unless you choose their hosted service. Note that captures of logged-in sessions will contain session material — treat output as sensitive.
alternatives: Browsertrix (platform) for a managed, team-scale version of the same crawler
brozzler for a distributed Internet-Archive-aligned alternative
ArchiveWeb.page for manual one-page capture by a non-engineer
summary: Dockerised browser-based crawler that drives Chromium to produce high-fidelity WARC/WACZ captures, with configurable scope…

name: Browsertrix
purpose: Multi-user web-archiving platform that orchestrates browsertrix-crawler on Kubernetes, with crawl scheduling, quality assurance review, collection management, replay and organisation-level access control.
journalism_use_case: Team-scale archiving programme where multiple reporters schedule crawls and share replayable collections — the step up from one engineer running captures to a newsroom where anyone can preserve a source and everyone can browse what has been preserved.
pros: Solves the organisational problem rather than the technical one: scheduling, shared collections and access control are what make archiving a newsroom capability instead of one person's habit
Built directly on browsertrix-crawler, so capture fidelity is the same as the standalone tool with none of the configuration burden pushed onto reporters
Quality-assurance review features let you check whether a capture actually worked before relying on it — a step most workflows skip
Very actively developed (v1.26.6 released 2026-11-05, pushed 2026-11-17) with AGPL-3.0 source available
cons: Kubernetes operational burden for self-hosting is substantial — realistically it needs someone who runs Kubernetes already, and small newsrooms usually end up on the paid hosted service instead
341 open issues, the largest backlog in the Webrecorder stack, reflecting the surface area of a full platform
If you use the hosted service, captures live in Webrecorder's infrastructure — a third-party custody decision that is fine for public material and not for confidential captures
S3-compatible storage plus a cluster means this is a platform commitment, not a tool you try casually
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 501 stars with 341 open issues, release v1.26.6 (2026-11-05), tag v1.27.0-beta.0, pushed 2026-11-17. The hosted service is Webrecorder's commercial offering, which is the realistic path for teams without Kubernetes capability — its pricing was not verified in this survey.
assessment: The right answer for a newsroom that has decided archiving is a programme, provided you can either run Kubernetes or accept hosted custody. For your profile I would be explicit about the split: hosted Browsertrix for public-interest preservation where third-party custody is acceptable, and self-hosted browsertrix-crawler for captures tied to confidential investigations. Trying to run the full platform without Kubernetes experience is the failure mode to avoid.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.26.6 (2026-11-05), tag v1.27.0-beta.0, 501 stars, 341 open issues. Same-day commits and frequent releases under a funded organisation; the large backlog is platform surface area rather than neglect.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified self-hosted instance offered to users obliges source publication — relevant if you customise it for partner organisations.
costs: Self-hosting: no software fee but a Kubernetes cluster plus S3-compatible storage — a four-figure annual infrastructure and ops commitment at minimum, dominated by staff time. Hosted Browsertrix is a paid service whose current prices were NOT verified in this survey — check the vendor before budgeting. Assumptions for self-hosting: small cluster, moderate capture volume.
privacy: Crawls and WACZ files are stored in your own cluster when self-hosted. On the hosted service they are held by Webrecorder — acceptable for public material, not for confidential captures. Organisation-level access control is a genuine benefit either way.
alternatives: browsertrix-crawler alone for engineer-run capture without the platform
ArchiveBox for a much lighter self-hosted team archive
Conifer for a hosted collection-oriented alternative — but note its slower cadence
blockers: Kubernetes requirement for self-hosting; hosted option places captures in third-party custody
summary: Multi-user web-archiving platform that orchestrates browsertrix-crawler on Kubernetes, with crawl scheduling…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure; staff effort

name: ArchiveWeb.page
purpose: Chromium browser extension and desktop app that records your browsing session into a WARC/WACZ archive, capturing exactly what you saw including pages behind authentication.
journalism_use_case: Manually capture a social post, story or logged-in page exactly as seen, producing a replayable file for the evidence locker — the only practical way to preserve content behind a login you legitimately hold, which automated crawlers cannot reach.
pros: Captures authenticated and interactive content that no crawler can reach, which covers a large share of what actually needs preserving (social posts, logged-in dashboards, paywalled filings)
Produces WACZ — the same evidentiary format as browsertrix-crawler — so manual captures sit alongside automated ones in one collection
Usable by a reporter with no technical skill: start recording, browse, export
Actively maintained (v0.17.1, 2026-09-04; pushed 2026-11-09) with a substantial community (1,629 stars)
cons: Manual, one-page-at-a-time workflow, so it does not scale and depends on reporter discipline at the moment of capture
Large captures strain browser storage, and losing an unexported archive to a browser profile reset is a real failure mode
Chromium-only, which is a constraint for newsrooms standardised on Firefox
AGPL-3.0 matters only if you redistribute a modified version; 115 open issues reflect the variety of sites users try to capture
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,629 stars with 115 open issues, release v0.17.1 (2026-09-04), pushed 2026-11-09. Part of the Webrecorder suite used across the web-archiving community.
assessment: Deploy it to reporters as the standard way to preserve anything they see that matters — the authenticated-capture capability has no real alternative. For your profile the operational rules are: export to a WACZ file immediately rather than leaving archives in the browser profile, and be aware that a capture of a logged-in session contains session material and personal account context, so handle the file as sensitive. Pair with ReplayWeb.page so colleagues can open captures without any setup.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-09, latest release v0.17.1 (2026-09-04), 1,629 stars, 115 open issues. Regular releases from a funded organisation; part of a coherently maintained suite.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Captured content belongs to the original publishers.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0; immaterial for ordinary use as an extension.
costs: Free. No infrastructure. Storage is local browser profile until exported.
privacy: The archive is stored in the browser profile until exported and nothing is uploaded by default — a strong privacy position. The caveat is the content: capturing a logged-in page records your session context, so exported files may contain account identifiers and should be treated accordingly.
alternatives: SingleFile for a lighter single-HTML snapshot (weaker provenance, no WARC)
Scoop for a provenance-attested single-page capture from the command line
browsertrix-crawler where the content is publicly reachable and automation is possible
summary: Chromium browser extension and desktop app that records your browsing session into a WARC/WACZ archive…

name: ReplayWeb.page
purpose: Browser-based, fully client-side viewer that opens WARC and WACZ archives and replays them without any server, using service workers.
journalism_use_case: Let editors, lawyers and readers open and inspect an archived page themselves, offline, from a single file — which is what converts a capture into usable evidence in an editorial or legal conversation, with no infrastructure between them and the material.
pros: Zero infrastructure and zero upload: hand someone a WACZ file and they can inspect it in a browser, which removes the single biggest practical barrier to using archived evidence
Client-side replay means the archive is never transmitted anywhere, so you can share a capture with a lawyer without it touching a server
Actively maintained (v2.5.4, 2026-10-22; pushed 2026-11-17) and part of the same suite that produces the captures
Can be embedded in a story page, so readers can examine the archived source themselves
cons: Fidelity is bounded by the original capture — ReplayWeb.page cannot show what was never recorded, and users often misattribute capture gaps to the viewer
Very large archives load slowly in a browser, so a multi-gigabyte collection is not a good fit for this path
AGPL-3.0 affects embedding a modified version in a distributed product
119 open issues, mostly replay edge cases on complex sites — the general hard problem of web-archive replay
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,015 stars with 119 open issues, release v2.5.4 (2026-10-22), pushed 2026-11-17. Widely used as the reference WACZ viewer across the web-archiving community.
assessment: Adopt — it is the piece that makes your captures socially useful. For your profile the highest-value application is legal and editorial review: a WACZ plus ReplayWeb.page lets counsel examine exactly what a page said without you building anything or exposing the archive. Embedding it in published stories is also worth considering where a source page is likely to change, since it lets readers verify your sourcing directly.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v2.5.4 (2026-10-22), 1,015 stars, 119 open issues. Same-day commits and current releases within the Webrecorder suite.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: embedding a modified version in a distributed product triggers source obligations. Using the hosted viewer or an unmodified self-hosted copy is unaffected.
costs: Free. No infrastructure; optionally self-host the static viewer alongside your archives.
privacy: Replay happens entirely client-side and archives are not uploaded — among the strongest privacy properties in this catalogue, and the reason it is safe to use for sensitive captures. If you use the hosted viewer, the page itself is loaded from Webrecorder but your archive file is not sent to them.
alternatives: pywb for server-side replay over a large collection
wabac.js to embed replay directly into your own application
OutbackCDX plus pywb for indexed access at scale
summary: Browser-based, fully client-side viewer that opens WARC and WACZ archives and replays them without any server…

name: wabac.js
purpose: JavaScript service-worker library that implements web-archive replay in the browser, providing the engine beneath ReplayWeb.page and ArchiveWeb.page.
journalism_use_case: Embed archive replay directly into a newsroom web application or story page without a replay server — for instance a story template where every cited source opens as its archived capture inline.
pros: Lets you build archive replay into your own product rather than iframing someone else's viewer, which matters for a newsroom with a custom publishing stack
Client-side by construction, so embedding it does not create a server-side archive-hosting liability
Actively maintained (v2.27.4, 2026-10-22; pushed 2026-11-13) and the same engine proven in ReplayWeb.page
Small, focused library with a clear purpose and a tiny issue backlog (16 open)
cons: Library-level component not used directly by journalists, so its value depends entirely on you building something around it
Requires a modern browser with service-worker support, and service-worker scope rules are a recurring source of integration difficulty
AGPL-3.0 on a component you embed in a published web application needs genuine legal consideration — this is the case where the licence actually bites
Tiny community (130 stars), so integration problems are yours to solve
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 130 stars with 16 open issues, release v2.27.4 (2026-10-22), pushed 2026-11-13. Its production use is evidenced by ReplayWeb.page and ArchiveWeb.page depending on it.
assessment: Only relevant if you are building a publishing feature around archived evidence — which is a genuinely good idea for an investigative outlet, since inline verifiable sources are a differentiator. Before committing, get a view on the AGPL question: embedding wabac.js in your public site is the scenario the licence is written for, and whether your site counts as a modified network service is a question for counsel, not for me. If that is a problem, ReplayWeb.page as a separate hosted viewer sidesteps it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-13, latest release v2.27.4 (2026-10-22), 130 stars, 16 open issues. Current releases within the Webrecorder suite; small but actively maintained.
licence_restrictions: Material here: embedding an AGPL-3.0 library in a public web application is precisely the network-service case the licence addresses. Take legal advice before shipping it in a proprietary publishing stack.
costs: No fee. No infrastructure (client-side). Cost is engineer integration time plus a legal review of the AGPL position.
privacy: Client-side only — the archive is processed in the reader's browser and not transmitted to your server, which is also a hosting-cost and liability advantage.
alternatives: ReplayWeb.page as a standalone viewer, avoiding the embedding question
pywb for server-side replay you control
A simple link to a downloadable WACZ plus instructions, which costs nothing
blockers: AGPL-3.0 embedding in a public web application — legal review required
summary: JavaScript service-worker library that implements web-archive replay in the browser…

name: browsertrix-behaviors
purpose: Library of site-specific and generic in-page behaviours (autoscroll, autoplay, expand-comments, platform-specific handlers) that run inside the capture browser to make dynamic content load before it is recorded.
journalism_use_case: Make automated captures of infinite-scroll social feeds and video pages actually complete, rather than capturing the first screen — the difference between archiving a post and archiving a post with its 400 comments.
pros: Directly addresses the main failure mode of automated social-media capture: content that only loads on interaction, which is most of what matters on a social post
Modular per-site behaviours mean a newsroom can write its own for a platform or portal that matters to its beat
Actively maintained in lockstep with the crawler (v0.16.0 released 2026-11-10, same-day push) with a tiny backlog (7 open issues)
AGPL-3.0 but used as a component inside your own capture pipeline, where the obligation is minimal
cons: Only as good as the per-site behaviour coverage: a platform without a behaviour, or one that has changed its markup, captures incompletely and often silently
Requires a browser capture host (Browsertrix or ArchiveWeb.page) — it does nothing standalone
Writing a new behaviour means reverse-engineering a platform's DOM, which is real work and breaks when the platform changes
Very small community (60 stars), so you are unlikely to find a third-party behaviour for a niche target
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 60 stars with 7 open issues, release v0.16.0 on 2026-11-10 with same-day push. Production use is evidenced by browsertrix-crawler's dependency on it.
assessment: You will use this implicitly through browsertrix-crawler rather than directly, and the reason to know it exists is operational: when a social capture comes out incomplete, the behaviour coverage is the thing to check and potentially extend. For your profile the actionable point is that writing a custom behaviour for a platform central to your reporting is a tractable piece of work with outsized evidentiary payoff — and worth doing before you need the capture, not after.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-10, latest release v0.16.0 published the same day, 60 stars, 7 open issues. Released in lockstep with the crawler it serves; small, focused and current.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0; minimal practical effect when used inside your own capture pipeline rather than redistributed.
costs: No fee. No separate infrastructure — it runs inside the capture browser. Cost is engineer time if you write custom behaviours.
privacy: Runs inside the capture browser; no separate data flows of its own.
alternatives: Manual capture with ArchiveWeb.page where a behaviour does not exist
Writing a custom behaviour for a platform central to your beat
Accepting partial captures and documenting the limitation in your methodology note
summary: Library of site-specific and generic in-page behaviours (autoscroll, autoplay, expand-comments, platform-specific handlers)…

name: Conifer
purpose: Web-archiving platform providing remote-browser capture sessions and organised, replayable collections, available as a hosted service or self-hosted Docker stack.
journalism_use_case: Capture a dynamic page or social feed through a remote browser session and keep it in an organised, replayable collection — the remote-browser aspect means the capture originates from Conifer's infrastructure rather than your own address, which can be useful when you do not want your newsroom IP visiting a target.
pros: Remote-browser capture provides a degree of separation between your network and the target, which is a genuine (if partial) operational-security benefit
Collection organisation and replay in one place, usable by non-engineers without any infrastructure
Apache-2.0 with a self-hostable Docker stack if you want the same model under your own control
Substantial community (1,549 stars) and an institutional home at Rhizome, with the repository transfer from webrecorder confirmed by redirect
cons: Slower cadence than Webrecorder's newer tools: last push 2026-07-22 (four months before this survey) with no release objects at all, and 128 open issues
Hosted quotas are small, so sustained use pushes you toward self-hosting or another tool
Captures are held by the hosted instance unless you self-host, which is a third-party custody decision
Superseded in practice by Browsertrix and ArchiveWeb.page for most use cases, so adopting it now means choosing the less-developed option
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: repository transfer webrecorder/conifer → Rhizome-Conifer/conifer confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17; 1,549 stars with 128 open issues; last push 2026-07-22; no release objects. The transfer plus slowing cadence is the significant pattern.
assessment: Hard to recommend for new work when ArchiveWeb.page covers manual capture and Browsertrix covers team-scale, both under faster maintenance. The one feature that still distinguishes Conifer is remote-browser capture, which has a real use when you want capture traffic not to originate from your network — though a dedicated VPS running browsertrix-crawler achieves the same with more control. Treat as a monitoring item, and note the transfer when updating any old links.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false (repository transferred to Rhizome-Conifer), pushed_at 2026-07-22, no release objects, 1,549 stars, 128 open issues. Four months without commits, no release engineering, and functional overlap with faster-moving tools from the original maintainer. Declining rather than dormant.
costs: Self-hosting: no fee, a Docker stack plus storage. Hosted conifer.rhizome.org has storage quotas; any paid tiers were not verified in this survey. Estimate for self-hosting: one moderate VM plus capture storage.
privacy: Captures are held by the hosted instance unless you self-host. The remote-browser model means the target sees Conifer's address rather than yours — a partial benefit, since the hosted operator then sees what you captured.
alternatives: ArchiveWeb.page for manual capture under your own control
Browsertrix for a maintained team platform
browsertrix-crawler on a dedicated VPS to get network separation with full control
summary: Web-archiving platform providing remote-browser capture sessions and organised, replayable collections…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: Scoop
purpose: Single-page capture engine that records a URL to WARC/WACZ with extensive provenance metadata — capture timestamps, DNS and certificate information, and optional cryptographic signing.
journalism_use_case: Capture a single official page at the moment you read it, with provenance metadata attached, so the capture stands up later as evidence of what the page said before a quiet edit — the closest thing in this catalogue to a notarised screenshot.
pros: Provenance metadata is the differentiator: capture-time DNS and certificate details plus optional signing make the capture harder to dispute than a plain WARC, let alone a screenshot
Built by Harvard LIL, whose work on Perma.cc gives it genuine credibility in legal-evidence contexts — relevant if a capture may end up in a filing
MIT licensed with current releases (0.7.0, 2026-09-25, same-day push) and a small, clean backlog (13 open issues)
Single-page scope keeps it simple and fast: one command, one evidential artefact
cons: Single-page scope by design — no crawling, scheduling, diffing or alerting, so it complements rather than replaces a crawler
The detailed signing and provenance formats were not individually verified in this survey beyond the maintainers' description, so treat the cryptographic strength as documented-but-unverified here
Node.js plus a Chromium-family browser, and replay still needs ReplayWeb.page or pywb
Small community (217 stars), so integration knowledge is limited to the project's own documentation
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 217 stars with 13 open issues, release 0.7.0 on 2026-09-25 with same-day push, MIT licence. Harvard LIL's broader work (Perma.cc) is well established in legal-citation preservation, which is relevant institutional context rather than direct evidence for Scoop.
assessment: Adopt it as the capture tool for the specific pages a story will cite — the provenance metadata is exactly what you want when a government later claims the page never said that. For your profile the workflow is: browsertrix-crawler for breadth, Scoop for the handful of pages that carry the story, both into one collection with ReplayWeb.page for review. I would verify the signing format details with the maintainers before relying on cryptographic attestation in a legal context, since this survey did not.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-25, latest release 0.7.0 published the same day, 217 stars, 13 open issues. Current releases under institutional maintenance at Harvard LIL; small but well-kept.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Captured content belongs to the original publisher.
costs: No fee. Node.js plus a browser; negligible per-capture cost. Storage for WACZ files.
privacy: Captures are written locally to files you control with no third-party submission by default — appropriate for sensitive targets. Your capture request is visible to the target site in the normal way.
alternatives: Perma.cc (hosted, from the same lab) where a public permanent citation link is wanted
ArchiveWeb.page for manual capture of authenticated pages
browsertrix-crawler for multi-page capture
summary: Single-page capture engine that records a URL to WARC/WACZ with extensive provenance metadata — capture timestamps…
